Types of Metrics
-----------------------
We support 2 types of metrics based on their aggregation semantics:
* **Distributive Metrics:** These are purely additive over a given set of data points.
  Examples: *count* of number of correct predictions; *sum* of output token lengths across queries.
* **Algebraic Metrics:** These are averages or proportions over a given set of data points. They can be decomposed into components that are individually distributive.
  Examples: *precision*, which counts number of correct predictions and total number of data points separately and then divides them; *mean rouge-1*, which averages per-example rouge-1 values that assesses overlap of tokens between generated text and ground truth text.

you must specify their type (algebraic or distributive) and value range as illustrated below.

API: Multi-Config Specification
===============
The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go.
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search,
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values.
RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes,
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding,
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other
user-defined knobs.
Knob Set Generators
-------
To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs
to generate groups of full configs.
We currently support two common knob set generators: List() for a discrete
set of values and Range() for sampling from a continuous value interval.
.. py:function:: List(values: List[Any])
	:param values: List of discrete values for a knob; all values must be the same python data type.
	:type values: List[Any]
.. py:function:: Range(start: int | float, end: int | float, dtype: str = "int" | "float")
	:param start: Lower bound of range interval.
	:type start: int | float
	:param end: Upper bound of range interval.
	:type end: int | float
	:param dtype: Data type of value to be sampled, either "int" or "float".
	:type dtype: str
**Notes:**
As of this writing, Range() performs uniform sampling within the given interval.
We plan to continue expanding this API and add more functionality on this front based on feedback.
Note that the return types of the knob set generators are internal to RapidFire AI and
they are usable only within the context of the config group generators below.
Config Group Generators
-----
We currently support two common config group generators: RFGridSearch() for grid search
and RFRandomSearch() for random search.
More support for AutoML heuristics such as SHA, HyperOpt, as well as an integration with

What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============
The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*,
and then cycles through all shards.
Suppose you have only 1 GPU, say an A100 or H100, and you want to run SFT on a Llama model.
Current tools force you to run one config after another *sequentially* as shown in the (simplified) illustration below.
In contrast, by operating on shards, RapidFire AI offers a far more concurrent learning experience by
automatically *swapping* adapters (and base models, if needed) across GPU(s) and DRAM.
It does this via efficient shared memory-based caching mechanisms that can spill to disk when needed.

   :width: 800px
In the above figure, all 3 model configs are shown for 1 epoch. RapidFire AI is set to use 4 chunks.
So, before model config 3 (M3) even starts in the sequential approach, RapidFire AI already shows you
the learning behaviors of all 3 configs on the first 2-3 chunks.
The overhead of swapping, represented by the thin gray box, is minimal, less than 5% of the runtime,
as per our measurements--thanks to our new efficient memory management techniques.
For inference evals for RAG/context engineering, such sharded execution means RapidFire AI surfaces eval metrics
sooner based on a statistical technique known as *online aggregation* from the database systems literature.
Basically, see estimated values and confidence intervals for all eval metrics in real time as the shards
get processed, ultimately converging to the exact metrics on the full dataset.
The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------
Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time

Following context lines 36-55:
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short.
*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior.

================
Overview
--------
An "Experiment" is the central concept in RapidFire AI to organize and streamline your multi-config AI experimentation.
Every experiment must have a unique user-given name that is used to collate plots on the ML metrics dashboard and for saving its artifacts.
If you (mistakenly) reuse a previous experiment name, RapidFire AI will append a suffix akin to what filesystems do.

As of this writing, an experiment can operate in either "fit" mode or "eval" mode but not both.

Dashboard: Interactive Control (IC) Ops
===============
Interactive Control Operations (IC Ops) are a powerful differentiating aspect of RapidFire AI
that enable *rapid experimentation* capability for AI customization.
Motivation for IC Ops
----
IC Ops are control operations over the runs *in flight* in an ongoing experiment.
They are motivated by an often under-appreciated pain point felt by many AI developers:
* How accurate a given configuration will be is *impossible* to tell upfront in general. Experimentation is critical: one must try alternate configs based on their intuition about their specific use case, dataset, model, and eval metrics.
* Not all configs are made equal. One must be able to easily try and retry values, zoom into promising regions of values, adjust on the fly, etc. This can help reach better eval metrics/model alignment more quickly. Otherwise, one might squander their (labeled) data and/or waste resources.
* Even for a prior deployed model, one may need to adapt knobs over time as the data distribution evolves (e.g., concept drift), application schema evolves (e.g., data collection process changes), newer/better models emerge (e.g., smaller but more capable LLMs), etc.
Generic MLOps tools treat a run as a generic monolithic job and schedule them at a coarse granularity,
leading to a disconnect between what is needed for customization and the execution layer.
IC Ops alter this status quo by giving you a whole new level of control over runs in flight.
No need to juggle disparate tools for data-parallelism (DDP), model-parallelism (FSDP / DeepSpeed), or
task-parallelism (W&B, Ray Tune, etc.).
RapidFire AI's execution engine handles lower level scheduling and orchestration of run adaptively
to enable IC Ops.
Semantics of IC Ops
-----
IC Ops can be used only when a run_fit() is actively running.
To access the IC Ops panel, click on the "IC Ops" column buttons in the runs table
or on any run's curve on any metrics plot in the "Chart" view.

External Vector Stores: Pinecone and PGVector
-------
RapidFire AI also supports external persistent vector stores beyond the default in-memory FAISS.
This allows you to scale to larger corpora, persist indexes across runs and experiments, and leverage managed vector DBMS services.
As of this writing, **Pinecone** (hosted serverless or pod-based) and **PostgreSQL PGVector** (self-hosted or managed) are supported.
Each external store supports three modes of operation:
- **Create mode:** Build a new index from base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG.
- **Read mode:** Retrieve from a pre-existing index and use it for RAG.
- **Update mode:** Add new content to an existing index from additional base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG.
See the API: LangChain RAG Spec page</ragspecs> for more details on how to specify these external vector stores.
The FiQA RAG tutorial notebooks have also been extended to showcase the external stores as below:
- **Pinecone**: View on GitHub <https://github.com/RapidFireAI/rapidfireai/blob/main/tutorial_notebooks/rag-contexteng/rf-tutorial-rag-fiqa-pinecone.ipynb>__
- **PGVector**: View on GitHub <https://github.com/RapidFireAI/rapidfireai/blob/main/tutorial_notebooks/rag-contexteng/rf-tutorial-rag-fiqa-pgvector.ipynb>__

-------
We compare 2 generator model sizes: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct.

32-token overlap using recursive character splitting with tiktoken encoding.
The RAG pipeline uses:

with a simple grid search: 2 generator models x 2 chunk sizes x 2 reranking top-n values.

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================
When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results.
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config
yields poor eval metrics.
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved,
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.
RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation**
from database systems research to LLM evals.
Our adaptive execution engine, as described on this page</difference>, automatically
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with
efficient swapping techniques.
This means you get **running metric estimates with confidence intervals** in real time.
So, you can confidently stop poor configs earlier, clone better configs on the fly, and
perform more informed exploration to reach much better eval metrics in much less time.
Example: Traditional Batch Evals vs. RapidFire AI
-------
For instance, suppose you have an evals set with 400 queries. You decide to compare, say,
4 RAG configs in one go with RapidFire AI with number of shards set to 8. The illustration
below contrasts traditional batch evals vs. RapidFire AI's approach for a simple eval metric.
.. list-table::
   :widths: 50 50
   :class: side-by-side
   * - .. figure:: /images/rag-eval-online1.png
          :width: 100%
          :alt: Online aggregation for evals with RapidFire AI and IC Ops.
     - .. figure:: /images/rag-eval-online2.png
          :width: 100%
          :alt: Online aggregation for evals with RapidFire AI and IC Ops.
All configs are executed on the first 1/8th of the data (50 examples), with
their **incrementally computed** eval metrics shown in real time with confidence intervals.
In the figure, the 3 worst configs are stopped, while the best is cloned to add 2 new variants.

100 examples), and so on.
One clone is then stopped halfway through the aggregation, while the other two run to completion.

API: LoRA and Model Configs
===============
RapidFire AI's core APIs for model and adapter specifications are all thin wrappers around
the corresponding APIs of the Hugging Face's libraries
transformers <https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/index>__
and PEFT LoRA <https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/developer_guides/lora>__.
RFLoraConfig
------
This is a wrapper around LoraConfig in HF PEFT.
The full signature and list of arguments are available on this page
<https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/v0.17.0/en/package_reference/lora#peft.LoraConfig>__.
The difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be List valued or
Range valued in a RFLoraConfig.
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can
be produced. Also read the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>.
**Example:**
.. code-block:: python
    # Singleton config
    RFLoraConfig(
        r=128, lora_alpha=256, lora_dropout=0.05,
        target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"], bias="none"
    )
    # 4 combinations
    RFLoraConfig(
        r=List([16, 32]), lora_alpha=List([16,32]), lora_dropout=0.05,
        target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"], bias="none"
    )
    # 2 combinations
    RFLoraConfig(
        r=64, lora_alpha=128,
        target_modules=List([["q_proj", "v_proj"],
        ["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"]]),
        bias="none"
    )
**Notes:**
In terms of impact on LLM behavior, the LoRA knobs that are usually experimented with are as follows:
* r (rank): The most critical knob. Typically a power of 2 between 8 and 128. Higher rank means higher adapter learning capacity but slightly higher GPU memory footprint and compute time.
* lora_alpha: Controls adaptation strength. Typical values are 16, 32, and 64. Usually set to 2x r, but this can be varied too.
* target_modules: Which layers to apply LoRA to. Common options:
  * Query/Value only: ["q_proj", "v_proj"]
  * Query/Key/Value: ["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj"]
  * All linear layers: ["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"]
* lora_dropout:  Controls regularization. Typically between 0.0 to 0.05; often set at 0.0 unless there is overfitting.
* init_lora_weights: Initialization strategy. Most use default True but some experiment with "gaussian" or newer methods such as "pissa".
Most other knobs such as bias, use_rslora, modules_to_save, etc. can be left as PEFT defaults unless you want to explore specific advanced variations.
A common combination is to start with rank 16 and 32 (resp. alpha 32 and 64) and only target query/value projection modules. Then expand to more based on observed loss and eval metrics behavior (overfitting or underfitting) and your time/compute constraints.

Known Issues and Updates Coming Soon
=============
As of this writing, RapidFire AI has the following known issues. We have listed some
recommended recourses for some.
We are actively working on resolving these and welcome feedback on their utility for your
use cases to help with prioritization.
Multi-GPU Model Support
------
Ordinarily, any given run's model(s) for its batch size must fit on a single GPU's memory.
For DPO and GRPO, both the policy and reference models must fit on the GPU together.
For SFT (and DPO), RapidFire AI can use FSDP automatically to partition a large model across GPUs on the same machine.
Provide the FSDP usage details in a config knob. See the SFT page</sft> FSDP section for more deatils.
Support for GRPO coming soon.
We also plan to add support for multi-GPU model partitioning via DeepSpeed soon.
ImportError in between Experiments
------
If you run multiple experiments back to back from the same notebook/IDE session, you might
see the following error appear occasionally:
.. code-block:: python
   ImportError: cannot import name 'GenerationMixin' from 'transformers.generation'
This is caused by stray Python processes from the previous experiment not ending properly.
If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:
* Run the command ps - ef | grep python, look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes, and kill if there are any with command kill -9 [PID].
* Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill as above.
* Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.
Recovering Storage Space
-------
If you run out of storage space on your machine due to experimenting with lots of LLMs, we
recommend clearing out the ".cache" folder on your home directory that is created by
Hugging Face to import the base models.
One experiment's imported models are not needed for another; so, it is safe to delete them.
If you want to reclaim even more space, look at the artifacts from your experiments and

Following context lines 51-66:
either delete some of the files or move them to other/remote storage.
Note that when you use LoRA adapters, RapidFire AI saves only the trained adapters in the
checkpoints of the runs, not the base models.
Semi-Automated IC Ops
------
Triggering IC Ops manually from the dashboard is feasible only if there is a human in the loop.
But IC Ops are useful even in offline scripted settings based on application logic, e.g., stop
90% of runs with poor eval metrics and clone-modify the top 10% to drill down into more
fine-grained values for their knobs.
In the near future, we plan to update the Experiment API to let you specify such custom
semi-automation logic for IC Ops in code using the runs' metrics and progress so far.

* **Distributive Metrics:** These are purely additive over a given set of data points.
  Examples: *count* of number of correct predictions; *sum* of output token lengths across queries.
* **Algebraic Metrics:** These are averages or proportions over a given set of data points. They can be decomposed into components that are individually distributive.
  Examples: *precision*, which counts number of correct predictions and total number of data points separately and then divides them; *mean rouge-1*, which averages per-example rouge-1 values that assesses overlap of tokens between generated text and ground truth text.

API: User-Provided Functions for Run Fit
===============
Apart from the classes to define models, adapters, and trainers, users can create the following custom
functions as part of their experiments.
Create Model Function
------
Mandatory user-provided function to create HuggingFace model and tokenizer objects based on the
model type(s) and name(s) given in the RFModelConfig and multi-config specification.
Also read the LoRA and Model Configs page</models>.
A model can be imported from the Hugging Face model hub or read from a local checkpoint file.
It is passed to run_fit() directly. Also read the Experiment page</experiment>.
This function is invoked when a trainer object is created for each run.
.. py:function:: create_model_fn(model_config: Dict[str, Any]) -> Tuple[transformers.PreTrainedModel, transformers.PreTrainedTokenizer]
  :param model_config: Dictionary injected by RapidFire AI into this user-defined function with all key-value pairs for one model config output by the config-group generator.
  :type model_config: Dict[str, Any]
  :return: Tuple containing the initialized Hugging Face model (e.g., AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoModelForSequenceClassification) and tokenizer (e.g., AutoTokenizer, PreTrainedTokenizer) objects
  :rtype: Tuple[transformers.PreTrainedModel, transformers.PreTrainedTokenizer]
**Example:**
.. code-block:: python
	# From the SFT tutorial notebook
	def sample_create_model(model_config):
    	"""Function to create model object for any given config; must return tuple of (model, tokenizer)"""
		from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM, AutoModelForMaskedLM
		model_name = model_config["model_name"]
		model_type = model_config["model_type"]
		model_kwargs = model_config["model_kwargs"]
		if model_type == "causal_lm":
			model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, **model_kwargs)
		elif model_type == "seq2seq_lm":
			model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(model_name, **model_kwargs)
		elif model_type == "masked_lm":
			model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(model_name, **model_kwargs)
		elif model_type == "custom":
            # Handle custom model loading logic, e.g., loading your own checkpoints
            # model = ...
			pass
		else:
			# Default to causal LM
			model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, **model_kwargs)
		tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
		return (model,tokenizer)

        responses = [completion[0]['content'] for completion in completions]

    def strict_format_reward_func(completions, **kwargs) -> list[float]:
        """Reward function that checks if the completion has a specific format."""
        import re
        pattern = r"^<reasoning>\n.*?\n</reasoning>\n<answer>\n.*?\n</answer>\n$"
        responses = [completion[0]["content"] for completion in completions]

API: Trainer Configs
===============
RapidFire AI's core APIs for trainer specifications are all thin wrappers around the
corresponding APIs of Hugging Face's TRL <https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/index>__ libraries.
RFSFTConfig
------
This is a wrapper around SFTConfig in HF TRL.
The full signature and list of arguments are available on this page
<https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/sft_trainer#trl.SFTConfig>__.
The only difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be List valued
or Range valued in RFSFTConfig.
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can be
produced. Also read the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>.
Other than the multi-config specification, this class preserves all semantics of Hugging Face's
SFT trainer under the hood.

	# From the SFT tutorial notebook
	RFSFTConfig(

		lr_scheduler_type = "linear",
		per_device_train_batch_size=4,
		per_device_eval_batch_size=8,
		gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
		num_train_epochs=2,
		logging_steps=5,
		eval_strategy="steps",
		eval_steps=25,
		fp16=True,
		save_strategy="epoch",
	)
	# Two knobs have list values here
	RFSFTConfig(
		learning_rate=List([2e-4, 1e-5]),
		lr_scheduler_type=List(["linear", "cosine"]),
		per_device_train_batch_size=4,

API: User-Provided Functions for Run Evals
===============
Users can provide the following custom functions as part of their eval config to be used in run_evals().
Note that each leaf config can have its own set of functions for all of these.
Preprocess Function
-------------------
Mandatory user-provided function to prepare the inputs to be given to the generator model.
It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process before generation.
Pass it directly to the preprocess_fn key in your eval config dictionary.
The system injects into this function the batch data, as well as the RAG spec and
the prompt manager of an individual leaf config.
.. py:function:: preprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list], rag: RFLangChainRagSpec, prompt_manager: RFPromptManager) -> dict[str, list]
   :param batch: Dictionary with a batch of examples with dataset field names as keys and lists as values
   :type batch: dict[str, list]
   :param rag: RAG specification object for document chunk retrieval and context serialization
   :type rag: RFLangChainRagSpec
   :param prompt_manager: Prompt manager object for handling instructions and few-shot examples
   :type prompt_manager: RFPromptManager
   :return: Dictionary with the preprocessed batch. It must have a reserved key "prompts" for the fully formatted prompts for the generator. Other key-value pairs from the original batch can also be copied over if you want.
   :rtype: dict[str, list]

		# Extract the retrieved document ids from the context.

If you run out of storage space on your machine due to experimenting with lots of LLMs, we
recommend clearing out the ".cache" folder on your home directory that is created by
Hugging Face to import the base models.
One experiment's imported models are not needed for another; so, it is safe to delete them.
If you want to reclaim even more space, look at the artifacts from your experiments and
either delete some of the files or move them to other/remote storage.
Note that when you use LoRA adapters, RapidFire AI saves only the trained adapters in the
checkpoints of the runs, not the base models.
Semi-Automated IC Ops
------
Triggering IC Ops manually from the dashboard is feasible only if there is a human in the loop.
But IC Ops are useful even in offline scripted settings based on application logic, e.g., stop
90% of runs with poor eval metrics and clone-modify the top 10% to drill down into more
fine-grained values for their knobs.
In the near future, we plan to update the Experiment API to let you specify such custom
semi-automation logic for IC Ops in code using the runs' metrics and progress so far.

If you run multiple experiments back to back from the same notebook/IDE session, you might
see the following error appear occasionally:
.. code-block:: python
   ImportError: cannot import name 'GenerationMixin' from 'transformers.generation'
This is caused by stray Python processes from the previous experiment not ending properly.
If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:
* Run the command ps - ef | grep python, look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes, and kill if there are any with command kill -9 [PID].
* Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill as above.
* Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

Task, Dataset, and Prompt

This tutorial shows Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for creating a customer support Q&A chatbot.
It uses the "Bitext customer support" dataset;
see its details on Hugging Face <https://huggingface.co/datasets/bitext/Bitext-customer-support-llm-chatbot-training-dataset>__.

The lite version uses only one: TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0.
There are 2 different LoRA adapter configurations: a low-capacity adapter (rank 16; 8 for lite) targeting

=======================
Please check out the tutorial notebooks on the links below. Right click on the GitHub link to save that file locally.
DPO for alignment: View on GitHub <https://github.com/RapidFireAI/rapidfireai/blob/main/tutorial_notebooks/post-training/rf-tutorial-dpo-alignment.ipynb>__.

Use this version if your GPU has < 80 GB HBM; it just uses smaller LLMs and finishes faster.
Task, Dataset, and Prompt
-------
This tutorial shows Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for aligning LLMs with human preferences.
DPO is a simpler alternative to PPO that directly optimizes the policy model using preference
data without requiring a separate reward model.
It uses the "ultrafeedback binarized" dataset;
see its details on Hugging Face <https://huggingface.co/datasets/trl-lib/ultrafeedback_binarized>__.
We use a sample of 500 training examples for tractable demo runtimes.
The dataset contains paired preference data with chosen (preferred) and rejected (dispreferred)
responses for the same prompts.
The training starts from a pre-trained SFT model (rapidfire-ai-inc/mistral-7b-sft-bnb-4bit)
to ensure the model distribution is suitable for DPO alignment training.
Model, Adapter, and Trainer Knobs
-------
We use the Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 base model fine-tuned with 4-bit quantization (QLoRA).
There are 4 different DPO training configurations exploring various loss functions and hyperparameters:
* Basic Bradley-Terry: Standard sigmoid loss with medium capacity LoRA (rank 64) and large beta.
* High divergence: High capacity LoRA (rank 128) with small beta to encourage divergence from reference model.
* Robust loss: Uses robust loss type with label smoothing to handle noisy preference data.
* Combined loss: Weighted combination of sigmoid, BCO pair, and SFT losses.
All configurations use QLoRA with the same target modules and are launched with a simple grid search,
totaling 4 combinations.
The lite version simply uses a smaller LoRA rank of 16 and a subset of 3 configs from the above list.

This tutorial shows Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to improve mathematical reasoning capabilities.

It uses the GSM8K mathematical reasoning dataset;
see its details on Hugging Face <https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k>__.
We use a sample of 500 training examples and 100 evaluation examples for tractable demo runtimes.

and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, all using 4-bit quantization for efficient training.
All models use the same medium capacity LoRA configuration, targeting only 2 modules.

There are 5 custom reward functions that collectively shape the model's behavior.
The whole set of reward functions is used for all configs.

It uses the "SciFact" dataset from the BEIR benchmark;

The dataset contains scientific claims that must be labeled as SUPPORT, CONTRADICT, or NOINFO based on retrieved evidence.

Model, RAG Components, and Configuration Knobs
-------

The RAG pipeline uses:
- **Embeddings**: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small.
- **Vector Store**: FAISS with CPU-based exact search, i.e., no ANN approximation.
- **Chunking**: 512-token chunks with 32-token overlap using recursive character splitting with tiktoken encoding.
- **Retrieval**: Top-15 initial retrieval.
- **Reranking**: cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 with top-5 final documents.
- **Document Template**: Custom template including document titles with content.
All other knobs are fixed across all configs. Thus, there are a total of 4 combinations launched
with a simple grid search: 2 generator models x 2 search strategies.

Overview of RapidFire AI Package
==============
RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms your LLM pipeline customization
from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution,
dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization.
For *RAG and context engineering evals*, start here: Install and Get Started: RAG and Context Engineering</walkthroughrag>.
For *SFT and RFT/post-training workflows*, start here: Install and Get Started: SFT/RFT</walkthroughft>.
RapidFire AI is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between the IDE
where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend.

   :width: 800px
Just pip install the rapidfireai OSS package. It works on a CPU-only machine, a single-GPU machine,
or a multi-GPU machine. Note that for RAG/context engineering with only closed model APIs, GPUs are not needed.
Launch the server from the command line. Then import it as any other python package in your notebook/script.
Use our API to define and launch the configs to compare in one go.
Metrics plots are automatically visualized in the ML metrics dashboard (for SFT/RFT only for now) or shown in an
in-notebook take (for RAG/context eng. only for now).

**Result**: Runtime cut by *4.7x*, alongside likely *better eval metrics*.
Of course, batch evals is also *embarrassingly parallel*. So, if you are able to use, say,
10 machines for the above workload, the two runtimes will come down to 107min vs. 23min.
Note that apart from time, on closed model APIs, your token spend is also reallocated
to more productive configs, which offers better return on investment for your use case.
Why Not Just Downsample?
------------------------
One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here.
As also explained on this page</difference>, downsampling alone has
significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI.
First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually
over and over, but that adds manual grunt work of juggling separate samples/files.
Finally, downsampling alone does not offer you the power of IC Ops and automated
parallelization to try new configs on the fly--you'd have reimplement those manually.
RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach with IC Ops avoids all the above issues,
while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in
conjunction for even lower runtimes/costs.
Takeaways
----------
RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process.
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control,
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.

Example Impact with IC Ops
-------
Returning to our above example, suppose we have an evals set with 400 queries. We compare
16 RAG configs (say, 2 retrieval, 2 reranking, and 4 prompting schemes) with 8 shards.
Let us say it takes 10s on average per query. And you run this on one machine.
**Traditional Batch Evals**: You explore the configs sequentially, one after another.
Total time taken: 16 configs x 400 queries x 10s/query = **17.8 hours**
**RapidFire AI**: Suppose you stop the worst 15 configs after the first shard based
on the projected estimates and confidence intervals;
then clone the best config and add 4 new variants then stop the worst 4 configs
after the second shard; then let only the best config continue till the last shard.
Total time taken: 16 * (400/8) * 10s + 5 * (400/8) * 10s + 1 * (6 * 400/8) * 10s = **3.8 hours**

Known Issues and Updates Coming Soon
=============
As of this writing, RapidFire AI has the following known issues. We have listed some
recommended recourses for some.
We are actively working on resolving these and welcome feedback on their utility for your
use cases to help with prioritization.
Multi-GPU Model Support
------
Ordinarily, any given run's model(s) for its batch size must fit on a single GPU's memory.
For DPO and GRPO, both the policy and reference models must fit on the GPU together.
For SFT (and DPO), RapidFire AI can use FSDP automatically to partition a large model across GPUs on the same machine.
Provide the FSDP usage details in a config knob. See the SFT page</sft> FSDP section for more deatils.
Support for GRPO coming soon.
We also plan to add support for multi-GPU model partitioning via DeepSpeed soon.
ImportError in between Experiments
------
If you run multiple experiments back to back from the same notebook/IDE session, you might
see the following error appear occasionally:
.. code-block:: python
   ImportError: cannot import name 'GenerationMixin' from 'transformers.generation'
This is caused by stray Python processes from the previous experiment not ending properly.
If you see this error, we recommend the following steps:
* Run the command ps - ef | grep python, look for "multiprocessing.spawn"/"defunct" processes, and kill if there are any with command kill -9 [PID].
* Wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there are processes to kill as above.
* Restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.
Recovering Storage Space
-------
If you run out of storage space on your machine due to experimenting with lots of LLMs, we
recommend clearing out the ".cache" folder on your home directory that is created by
Hugging Face to import the base models.
One experiment's imported models are not needed for another; so, it is safe to delete them.
If you want to reclaim even more space, look at the artifacts from your experiments and

Following context lines 51-66:
either delete some of the files or move them to other/remote storage.
Note that when you use LoRA adapters, RapidFire AI saves only the trained adapters in the
checkpoints of the runs, not the base models.
Semi-Automated IC Ops
------
Triggering IC Ops manually from the dashboard is feasible only if there is a human in the loop.
But IC Ops are useful even in offline scripted settings based on application logic, e.g., stop
90% of runs with poor eval metrics and clone-modify the top 10% to drill down into more
fine-grained values for their knobs.
In the near future, we plan to update the Experiment API to let you specify such custom
semi-automation logic for IC Ops in code using the runs' metrics and progress so far.

Types of Metrics
-----------------------
We support 2 types of metrics based on their aggregation semantics:
* **Distributive Metrics:** These are purely additive over a given set of data points.
  Examples: *count* of number of correct predictions; *sum* of output token lengths across queries.
* **Algebraic Metrics:** These are averages or proportions over a given set of data points. They can be decomposed into components that are individually distributive.
  Examples: *precision*, which counts number of correct predictions and total number of data points separately and then divides them; *mean rouge-1*, which averages per-example rouge-1 values that assesses overlap of tokens between generated text and ground truth text.

reference_answer: RapidFire AI currently supports two knob set generators: List() for a discrete set of values and Range() for sampling from a continuous value interval. List() takes a list of discrete values where all values must be the same Python data type. Range() takes a start, end, and dtype parameter (either 'int' or 'float') and performs uniform sampling within the given interval.

Traditional tools force you to run one config after another sequentially. In contrast, RapidFire AI's adaptive execution engine shards the dataset randomly into chunks and schedules all runs on one shard at a time, then cycles through all shards. This enables interruptible execution across GPUs/CPUs, providing a far more concurrent learning experience by automatically swapping adapters and base models across GPUs and DRAM via efficient shared memory-based caching mechanisms. The swapping overhead is minimal, less than 5% of runtime. This means before the third model config even starts in the sequential approach, RapidFire AI already shows learning behaviors of all configs on the first 2-3 chunks.

The Experiment constructor accepts three parameters: (1) experiment_name (str), a unique name for the experiment used to collate plots on the dashboard and for saving artifacts; (2) mode (str), either 'fit' or 'eval' with default 'fit'; and (3) experiments_path (str, optional), the path to a folder to store experiment artifacts, defaulting to './rapidfire_experiments'.

RFGridSearch requires each knob to have either a single value or a List() of values, but no knob should have a Range() of values or it will error out. RFRandomSearch allows each knob to have a single value, a List() of values, or a Range() of values. Its sampling semantics are independently-identically-distributed (IID): it uniformly randomly picks a value from each discrete set and from each continuous set to construct one knob combination, then repeats this process to accumulate num_runs distinct combinations.

For RAG/context engineering with only closed model APIs (like OpenAI), GPUs are not needed. Install RapidFire AI with 'pip install rapidfireai' (requires Python 3.12+), then run 'rapidfireai init --evals' to initialize for RAG evals, and then 'rapidfireai start' to start the server. Starting the server is optional for run_evals() since results are also shown in an in-notebook table and IC Ops can be displayed in the notebook. Provide a valid OpenAI API key via a config argument as shown in the GSM8K and SciFact tutorial notebooks.

RapidFire AI supports four IC Ops: (1) Stop - earmarks a run to be stopped at the end of its current chunk, keeping it alive but not using GPU resources from the next chunk; (2) Resume - applicable only to previously stopped runs, earmarks them to be resumed from the next chunk onward; (3) Clone-Modify - allows adding clones of a chosen parent run with editable config knobs, optionally warm-starting with the parent's weights; (4) Delete - earmarks a run to be deleted from the next chunk onward, making its curves vanish from the plots, though model checkpoints are preserved in the experiment artifacts.

The preprocess_fn is a mandatory user-provided function that prepares the inputs to be given to the generator model. It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process before generation. The system injects three arguments: (1) batch - a dictionary with a batch of examples with dataset field names as keys and lists as values; (2) rag - an RFLangChainRagSpec object for document chunk retrieval and context serialization; (3) prompt_manager - an RFPromptManager object for handling instructions and few-shot examples. The function must return a dictionary with a reserved key 'prompts' containing the fully formatted prompts for the generator.

RapidFire AI supports three vector store backends: (1) FAISS - an in-memory store that is the default and requires no setup, but only supports Create mode since it is not persistent; (2) PGVector (PostgreSQL) - a persistent vector store that supports Create, Read, and Update modes; (3) Pinecone - a cloud-hosted persistent vector store that also supports Create, Read, and Update modes. In Read mode, you retrieve from a pre-existing index. In Update mode, you add new content to an existing index. Using PGVector or Pinecone in Read mode is especially useful for efficient experimentation since you preprocess and embed your corpus once and then run many retrieval/generation configurations against the same index.

The DataFrame returned by get_runs_info() contains the following columns: run_id, status, mlflow_run_id, completed_steps, total_steps, start_chunk_id, num_chunks_visited_curr_epoch, num_epochs_completed, error, source, ended_by, warm_started_from, and config (the full config dictionary).

The three supported search algorithm types are: (1) 'similarity' - standard cosine similarity search, which is the default; (2) 'similarity_score_threshold' - similarity search with a minimum score threshold (SST), which additionally accepts a 'score_threshold' parameter; (3) 'mmr' - Maximum Marginal Relevance search for diversity, which additionally accepts 'fetch_k' (number of documents to fetch before MMR reranking, default 20) and 'lambda_mult' (diversity parameter balancing relevance vs. diversity, default 0.5). All three types support a 'k' parameter for the number of documents to retrieve (default 5) and an optional 'filter' parameter.

Online aggregation is a technique adapted from database systems research that provides running metric estimates with confidence intervals in real time as shards of the evaluation dataset are processed. This enables stopping poor configs earlier and cloning better configs on the fly. RapidFire AI supports three confidence interval strategies: (1) Normal Approximation - the default strategy using the Central Limit Theorem, suitable for non-trivial sample sizes (n > 30); (2) Wilson Score - better for small sample sizes or metrics near 0/1 boundaries, more robust for extreme proportions; (3) Hoeffding Bounds - best for maximum safety with guaranteed coverage, making no distributional assumptions but producing typically loose intervals. All three support optional Finite Population Correction (FPC).

When using the Clone-Modify IC Op, you can warm-start a clone using its parent's weights by enabling the warm-start option. Warm-started clones inherit their parent's learning behavior so far and can reach better eval metrics faster. However, warm starting is only allowed if the clone has identical neural architecture as the parent, including LoRA adapters; otherwise, it will error out. You can edit other knobs such as learning rate in the clone, but the model architecture and LoRA configuration must match the parent's for warm starting to work.

The accumulate_metrics_fn is an optional user-provided function that aggregates algebraic eval metrics across all batches of data. It is invoked once at the very end of the evaluation process after all batches have been processed. If this function is not provided, all metrics returned by the compute_metrics_fn will be assumed to be distributive (i.e., summed across batches) by default. This function is needed when metrics require weighted averaging or other custom dataset-wide aggregation logic. The return dictionary can include optional keys 'is_algebraic', 'is_distributive', and 'value_range' to support online aggregation.

RapidFire AI's current default dashboard is a fork of the popular OSS tool MLflow. It also supports TensorBoard and Trackio for logging metrics. Support for Weights & Biases and CometML is coming soon. You can specify which dashboards to use in two ways: (1) via the server start command with 'rapidfireai start --tracking-backends [mlflow | tensorboard | trackio]'; or (2) via environment variables in your Python code/notebook by setting RF_MLFLOW_ENABLED, RF_TENSORBOARD_ENABLED, and RF_TRACKIO_ENABLED to 'true'. You can use any one, two, or all three dashboards simultaneously.

The key LoRA knobs typically experimented with are: (1) r (rank) - the most critical knob, typically a power of 2 between 8 and 128, where higher rank means higher adapter learning capacity but slightly higher GPU memory footprint; (2) lora_alpha - controls adaptation strength, typical values are 16, 32, and 64, usually set to 2x the rank; (3) target_modules - which layers to apply LoRA to, common options being query/value only ['q_proj', 'v_proj'], query/key/value, or all linear layers; (4) lora_dropout - controls regularization, typically between 0.0 to 0.05. A common starting combination is rank 16 and 32 (with alpha 32 and 64 respectively) targeting only query/value projection modules, then expanding based on observed loss and eval metrics behavior.

When constructing a config group with List() or Range(), if the assigned search k value is less than the assigned reranker top_n value, the combination is meaningless and will be omitted automatically by RapidFire AI. All other combinations create valid runs. For example, if k is List([5, 10]) and top_n is List([5, 6]), then in the 2x2 grid, the combination k=5 and top_n=6 will be automatically omitted but the other 3 combinations will be valid.

RapidFire AI requires Python 3.12+. You should verify that your shell's python3 resolves to Python 3.12 before creating the virtual environment. If you encounter any error, you can run the diagnostic command 'rapidfireai doctor' to get a complete diagnostic report covering the Python environment, relevant packages, GPU/CUDA status, and key environment variables.

The document_template is an optional function that formats each retrieved chunk for context injection into prompts. It accepts a single LangChain Document object and returns a formatted string. Multiple documents are separated by double newlines when serialized. If not provided, the default template formats each document by joining all metadata key-value pairs with semicolons, followed by a newline and the document's page_content. Users can provide custom templates to control what metadata fields are included, for example including only the document source or a title field that was ingested via metadata_func in the document loader.

Unlike run_fit() which returns None, run_evals() returns a dictionary with the run/config ID as the key. The value is a 2-tuple containing two dictionaries: one for all aggregated metrics and one for all cumulative metrics. Within an experiment, you can rerun run_evals() as many times as you want, and all runs will be overlaid on the same plots on the ML metrics dashboard. The function also supports providing various config combinations including single config dictionaries, lists of configs, or config group generator outputs like RFGridSearch() and RFRandomSearch().

RapidFire AI supports two types of generator configs: (1) RFvLLMModelConfig, which wraps around vLLM's config and SamplingParams classes for self-hosted open LLMs; and (2) RFOpenAIAPIModelConfig, which wraps around OpenAI's API client config and chat completion parameters for closed model LLM APIs. Support for additional generator plugins including Gemini and Claude APIs is planned. In both cases, individual arguments (knobs) can be List or Range valued for multi-config specification.

The sampling_params dictionary in RFvLLMModelConfig controls sampling behavior during text generation by vLLM. The recommended knobs include: 'temperature' (a float controlling randomness where lower values are more deterministic and 0.0 means greedy sampling, default 1.0), 'top_p' (a float controlling cumulative probability of top tokens to consider, must be in (0,1], default 1.0), and 'max_tokens' (maximum number of tokens to generate per output sequence). All knobs in this dictionary are passed to vLLM as-is, and vLLM uses its defaults for unspecified knobs.

RFOpenAIAPIModelConfig provides two rate limiting parameters: rpm_limit (requests per minute) and tpm_limit (tokens per minute) to the OpenAI API. These are used for throttling to avoid exceeding OpenAI API quotas. Users should check the rate limits published by OpenAI for details on their tier and the latest per-model limits. When using closed model APIs, RapidFire AI's scheduler automatically optimizes how CPU cores and token rate limits are apportioned across configs to avoid wastage of token spend on unproductive RAG configs.

RFPromptManager provides semantic similarity-based example selection to construct prompts with the most relevant examples for each input query. It uses an embedding_cfg to compute semantic similarity between examples and queries, where the embedding class (such as HuggingFaceEmbeddings or OpenAIEmbeddings) is specified as a dictionary with the class itself as value (not an instance). The example_selector_cls parameter determines the selection strategy - either SemanticSimilarityExampleSelector for pure similarity or MaxMarginalRelevanceExampleSelector for diversity. The k parameter controls how many examples to retrieve per query (default 3). Each example is formatted using an example_prompt_template with placeholders matching the keys in the example dictionaries.

Apart from the Generator, the following knobs can be included in the eval config dictionary: batch_size (number of examples per batch), preprocess_fn (mandatory function to preprocess a batch), postprocess_fn (optional function to postprocess a batch after generation), compute_metrics_fn (mandatory function to compute eval metrics per batch), accumulate_metrics_fn (optional function to aggregate algebraic metrics across batches; if not given, all metrics are assumed distributive), and online_strategy_kwargs (optional dictionary for online aggregation with keys 'strategy_name', 'confidence_level' defaulting to 0.95, and 'use_fpc' defaulting to True). Each of these knobs can also be a List() or Range() knob set generator.

The create_model_fn is a mandatory user-provided function that must return a tuple of (model, tokenizer), specifically a HuggingFace PreTrainedModel and PreTrainedTokenizer. It receives a model_config dictionary as input, which is injected by RapidFire AI with all key-value pairs for one model config output by the config-group generator. This function is invoked when a trainer object is created for each run. Inside it, users can use whatever knobs they set in the config group, such as model type or name, to instantiate a model accordingly. Models can be imported from the Hugging Face model hub or loaded from local checkpoint files.

Reward functions are user-provided functions needed for GRPO that evaluate generated outputs during training. TRL injects lists of prompts, completions, completion IDs, and trainer state as keyword arguments. Users can use only a subset of these in their reward function signature as long as they include **kwargs. Depending on the dataset format, prompts and completions will be either lists of strings (standard format) or lists of message dictionaries (conversational format). The return type must be a list of floats (one per completion), or None for examples where the reward function is not applicable. Multiple reward functions can be passed as a list to the reward_funcs argument of RFModelConfig, and multiple variants of these lists can be used as a List for multi-config specification.

RFSFTConfig is a wrapper around HuggingFace TRL's SFTConfig class that preserves all its semantics under the hood. The only difference is that individual arguments (knobs) can be List or Range valued for multi-config specification. Key configurable arguments include learning_rate, lr_scheduler_type, per_device_train_batch_size, per_device_eval_batch_size, gradient_accumulation_steps, num_train_epochs, logging_steps, eval_strategy, eval_steps, fp16/bf16, and save_strategy. For larger LLMs that need cross-GPU model partitioning, you can also specify FSDP configuration using the fsdp and fsdp_config arguments with settings like sharding strategy, auto-wrap policy, and offloading parameters.

Both RFDPOConfig and RFGRPOConfig are wrappers around their corresponding HuggingFace TRL classes (DPOConfig and GRPOConfig respectively). RFDPOConfig includes DPO-specific arguments such as model_adapter_name, ref_adapter_name, force_use_ref_model, loss_type (e.g., 'sigmoid'), beta (controlling divergence from reference model), max_prompt_length, and max_completion_length. RFGRPOConfig includes GRPO-specific arguments such as num_generations (number of generated completions per prompt) and similar training parameters. A key difference is that RFDPOConfig supports FSDP for cross-GPU partitioning, while out-of-the-box FSDP support for GRPO is still in the works as of this writing.

A leaf config is a single combination of knob values in a config dictionary. In a config dictionary, a knob's value can be a singleton or set-valued (using List or Range). When set-valued knobs are fed to a config-group generator method, each unique combination produced is called a leaf config. RapidFire AI instantiates one run per leaf config, and its values are injected via the model_config argument to the user's create_model_fn() function. A run is a central concept representing this single combination of configuration knob values, and RapidFire AI assigns each run a unique integer run_id within an experiment.

The main Experiments page on the dashboard has 4 main tabs: (1) Table - shows a view of an experiment with all its runs where each run represents one model with one set of config knob values; (2) Chart - shows metrics plots with one plot per metric spanning loss on training and evaluation sets as well as all named metrics from the compute_metrics() function; (3) Experiment Log - a continually appending message log displaying all operations run with RapidFire AI's API; (4) Interactive Control (IC) Log - a continually appending log specifically displaying all IC operations done via the IC Ops panels.

If you run out of storage space, RapidFire AI recommends clearing out the '.cache' folder on your home directory, which is created by Hugging Face to import base models. One experiment's imported models are not needed for another, so it is safe to delete them. For additional space, you can look at the artifacts from your experiments and delete or move them to other/remote storage. Notably, when using LoRA adapters, RapidFire AI saves only the trained adapters in the run checkpoints, not the base models, which keeps checkpoint sizes manageable.

The SFT tutorial uses the 'Bitext customer support' dataset for creating a customer support Q&A chatbot. It uses a sample of 5,000 training examples and 200 evaluation examples for tractable demo runtimes. The full version compares 2 base model architectures: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, while the lite version uses only TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0. There are 2 different LoRA adapter configurations: a low-capacity adapter (rank 16; 8 for lite) targeting 2 modules and a high-capacity adapter (rank 128; 32 for lite) targeting 4 modules, totaling 4 combinations launched with grid search.

The DPO tutorial explores 4 configurations using the Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 base model with 4-bit quantization (QLoRA): (1) Basic Bradley-Terry - standard sigmoid loss with medium capacity LoRA (rank 64) and large beta; (2) High divergence - high capacity LoRA (rank 128) with small beta to encourage divergence from the reference model; (3) Robust loss - uses robust loss type with label smoothing to handle noisy preference data; (4) Combined loss - a weighted combination of sigmoid, BCO pair, and SFT losses. The training starts from a pre-trained SFT model (rapidfire-ai-inc/mistral-7b-sft-bnb-4bit) to ensure the model distribution is suitable for DPO alignment training.

The GRPO tutorial uses 5 custom reward functions: (1) Correctness reward - awards 2.0 points for matching the ground truth answer exactly; (2) Integer reward - awards 0.5 points for producing numeric answers, validating output format; (3) Strict format reward - awards 0.5 points for exact XML formatting compliance; (4) Soft format reward - awards 0.5 points for flexible XML formatting with more lenient matching; (5) XML count reward - a fine-grained reward of up to 0.5 points for proper XML tag usage and structure. The whole set of reward functions is used for all configs, and GRPO uses multiple reward functions to provide richer training signals.

The SciFact tutorial uses an all-closed model API workflow (no GPU needed) with the following RAG components: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small for embeddings, FAISS with CPU-based exact search (no ANN approximation) as the vector store, 512-token chunks with 32-token overlap using recursive character splitting with tiktoken encoding, top-15 initial retrieval, cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 reranker with top-5 final documents, and a custom document template including document titles with content. It compares 2 generator models via OpenAI API (gpt-5-mini and gpt-4o) across 2 different retrieval/search strategies (similarity search and MMR), for a total of 4 combinations launched with grid search.

The GSM8K tutorial uses a hybrid workflow with a self-hosted open LLM for embeddings and OpenAI API calls for generation. The few-shot prompting pipeline uses semantic similarity-based example selection with sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, drawn from a pool of 10 hand-crafted examples covering diverse problem types. It uses chain-of-thought style prompt templates with step-by-step reasoning and final answers after '####'. It compares 2 generator models (gpt-5-mini and gpt-4o), with 2 different reasoning effort levels (medium and high) for gpt-5-mini only, and 2 different few-shot k values (3 and 5 examples per prompt). This produces 6 total combinations via a union of two grids: 1x1x2 + 1x2x2 = 6.

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms LLM pipeline customization from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization. It is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between: the IDE where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend. It works on a CPU-only machine, a single-GPU machine, or a multi-GPU machine, and for RAG/context engineering with only closed model APIs, GPUs are not needed.

RapidFire AI provides three RAG/context engineering tutorials, each demonstrating a different workflow type: (1) FiQA RAG Q&A chatbot - an all-local model workflow with self-hosted open models from Hugging Face for both embedding and generation; (2) SciFact RAG for scientific claim verification - an all-OpenAI workflow using OpenAI calls for both embedding and generation (no GPU needed); (3) GSM8K few-shot/context engineering for math reasoning - a hybrid workflow spanning a self-hosted open LLM for embeddings and OpenAI API calls for generation.

To install RapidFire AI for fine-tuning: (1) ensure Python 3.12+, create a virtual environment, and run 'pip install rapidfireai'; (2) run 'rapidfireai init' to initialize dependencies (only needed once for a new venv or when switching GPUs); (3) run 'rapidfireai start' to launch the frontend dashboard and API server. For gated models like Llama and Mistral, you need a Hugging Face token: install huggingface-hub with the CLI extra, run 'hf auth login --token YOUR_TOKEN', and request access on the gated models' Hugging Face pages. Alternatively, you can switch the model_name to a non-gated model. Approval for Llama models may take a few hours.

The postprocess_fn is an optional user-provided function to postprocess a batch of examples and their respective generated outputs, which are injected into this function by the system under the reserved key 'generated_text'. It is useful for extracting structured information from generations, adding ground truth data, or performing any transformations needed before computing metrics. It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process after generation and before metric computation. It is passed directly to the 'postprocess_fn' key in the eval config dictionary. For example, in the SciFact use case, it extracts SUPPORT/CONTRADICT/NOINFO labels from generated text using regex patterns.

RapidFire AI identifies several disadvantages of downsampling alone: (1) you must decide a downsample size upfront, which is non-trivial if eval metrics have high variance across examples; (2) a single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone LLMs; (3) point estimates without confidence intervals can give false confidence; (4) manual resampling adds grunt work of juggling separate samples and files; (5) it requires manual checkpoint management; (6) downsampling alone does not offer dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify) or automated parallelization to try new configs on the fly. However, downsampling is complementary to rapid experimentation - users can use both together, as the adaptive execution engine operates on downsampled datasets all the same.

The SFT tutorial provides three FSDP configurations for different model sizes: (1) FSDP Lite with TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 needs at least 2x A10 GPUs or equivalent (48 GB total HBM); (2) FSDP Regular with Qwen3-32B needs at least 4x A10 GPUs or equivalent (96 GB total HBM); (3) FSDP Large with Llama-3-70B-Instruct needs at least 8x A10 GPUs or equivalent (192 GB total HBM). Although the FSDP tutorials can work on A10 GPUs, RapidFire AI highly recommends using at least A100s or later GPUs with NVLink support for reasonable runtimes.

This ImportError ('cannot import name GenerationMixin from transformers.generation') is caused by stray Python processes from the previous experiment not ending properly. To resolve it: (1) run the command 'ps -ef | grep python' and look for 'multiprocessing.spawn' or 'defunct' processes, then kill them with 'kill -9 [PID]'; (2) wait for about 2 minutes regardless of whether there were processes to kill; (3) restart the kernel and then proceed with your new experiment.

RFModelConfig is a core class that unifies model loading, training configurations, and LoRA settings. Its arguments include: model_name (HuggingFace model identifier or local path), tokenizer (tokenizer identifier, optional), tokenizer_kwargs (additional tokenizer arguments), formatting_func (data preprocessing function, can be a List), compute_metrics (evaluation function, can be a List), peft_config (RFLoraConfig for LoRA, can be a List), training_args (RFSFTConfig, RFDPOConfig, or RFGRPOConfig), model_type (custom string, default 'causal_lm'), model_kwargs (additional model init parameters), ref_model_name (for DPO/GRPO reference model), ref_model_type, ref_model_kwargs, reward_funcs (for GRPO, can be a List), generation_config (text generation arguments), and num_gpus (GPUs per run). One RFModelConfig can have only one base model and one training control flow, but Lists of PEFT configs, formatting functions, eval metrics functions, and reward functions are supported.

Distributive metrics are purely additive over a given set of data points, such as count of correct predictions or sum of output token lengths across queries. Algebraic metrics are averages or proportions over a given set of data points that can be decomposed into components that are individually distributive, such as precision (which divides correct predictions by total data points) or mean rouge-1 (which averages per-example values). When defining eval metrics via compute_metrics_fn and accumulate_metrics_fn, users must specify their type (algebraic or distributive) and value range for online aggregation. Metrics without a type defined are displayed as-is without projected estimates or confidence intervals.

**Online aggregation** in RapidFire AI evals adapts the database‑research concept of *online aggregation* to LLM evaluation pipelines.  
Instead of waiting for an entire dataset to finish, RapidFire AI shards the data, runs multiple configs in parallel on one shard at a time, and continuously updates metric estimates **with confidence intervals** as each shard is processed. This lets you stop poor‑performing configs early, clone promising ones on the fly, and reach reliable metric estimates much faster.

`accumulate_metrics_fn` is an optional user‑provided callback that runs **once, after all batches have been processed**, to combine the per‑batch metric dictionaries produced by `eval.compute_metrics_fn`. It lets you implement custom dataset‑wide aggregation (e.g., weighted averaging, computing accuracy from “Correct” and “Total”, or any other algebraic combination) and to mark the resulting metrics with flags such as `is_algebraic`, `is_distributive`, and `value_range`.

Signature  

```python
def accumulate_metrics_fn(
    aggregated_metrics: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]
) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]:
    ...
```

* `aggregated_metrics` – a mapping from metric name → list of the per‑batch metric dicts (each containing at least the reserved key `"value"`).  
* Return – a dict mapping metric name → a dict that must contain `"value"` and may also include `"is_algebraic"`, `"is_distributive"`, and `"value_range"`.

**If it is not provided**  
The eval system assumes that **all metrics returned by `eval.compute_metrics_fn` are distributive**, meaning they can simply be summed across batches. No custom aggregation is performed; the framework will aggregate by summing the `"value"` fields of each batch.

**`document_template` in `RFLangChainRagSpec`**  
- The template is applied when the RAG spec serializes retrieved documents via `rag.serialize_documents(...)`.  
- For each document, the template determines how the document’s metadata and its text content are combined into a single string that is then inserted into the prompt.  

**Default behavior**  
- If you do **not** supply a custom `document_template`, RapidFire AI falls back to the built‑in template:  

```
"metadata:\ncontent"
```

- In other words, the serialized string for a document consists of the document’s metadata (as a string) followed by a newline (`\n`) and then the document’s raw content.  

**Custom template**  
- You can override this by providing your own `document_template` in the `RFLangChainRagSpec` (e.g., to include a title field or format metadata differently). The custom template will be used instead of the default when `rag.serialize_documents` is called.

**RFPromptManager** builds a prompt by picking the most relevant few‑shot examples for each incoming query.  
The selection works as follows:

1. **Embedding the text** – The manager uses the **`embedding_cfg`** you provide (e.g., `HuggingFaceEmbeddings` or `OpenAIEmbeddings`) to embed both the query and all candidate examples.  

2. **Choosing a selector** – You specify an **`example_selector_cls`**:
   * `SemanticSimilarityExampleSelector` → picks examples that are *most semantically similar* to the query.  
   * `MaxMarginalRelevanceExampleSelector` → picks examples that are both similar and *diverse* (max‑marginal‑relevance).

3. **Retrieving the top‑k examples** – The manager then asks the selector to return **`k`** examples (default = 3). These are the examples that will be inserted into the prompt via the optional `example_prompt_template`.

In short, RFPromptManager embeds the query and the candidate examples, runs either a semantic‑similarity or a max‑marginal‑relevance selector, and returns the top k (default 3) most relevant (or diverse) examples for each input.

A **leaf config** is a single, concrete sub‑section of an evaluation configuration.  
In RapidFire AI, an eval config can contain multiple leaf configs, each representing an individual evaluation scenario (or “run”).  

* Each leaf config can define its own set of user‑provided functions—such as `preprocess_fn`, `postprocess_fn`, etc.—that are injected into the evaluation pipeline.  
* When you call `run_evals()`, the system iterates over the leaf configs and executes a separate run for each one, using the functions and settings defined in that leaf config.  

Thus, a leaf config is the granular unit of configuration that drives a single evaluation run, and multiple leaf configs allow you to run many variations of an evaluation in one call to `run_evals()`.

RapidFire AI says that plain down‑sampling leaves you with several critical shortcomings that its online‑aggregation + IC‑Ops workflow eliminates:

* **You must pick a sample size in advance** – a non‑trivial decision when your evaluation metrics vary a lot across examples.  
* **Down‑sampled results are just point estimates**; they lack statistically‑sound confidence intervals, so you can be falsely confident about a configuration’s performance.  
* **Manual resampling is cumbersome** – you have to generate, store, and juggle many separate sample files if you want to try different sizes or repeats.  
* **No dynamic, on‑the‑fly experimentation** – down‑sampling gives you a static dataset, so you cannot automatically prune bad configs, clone promising ones, or launch new variants while the eval is running. All of that parallel, adaptive control (the “IC Ops” power) would have to be re‑implemented manually.

RapidFire AI’s online aggregation approach provides real‑time metrics, confidence intervals, and automated parallelization, avoiding these downsides while even being usable together with down‑sampling for further cost‑time savings.

**Distributive metrics** are *purely additive* over the data points that have been seen.  
- They can be summed directly as more shards are processed.  
- Example: a **count** of correct predictions or the **sum** of output‑token lengths.  

**Algebraic metrics** are *averages or proportions* that are computed from separate additive components.  
- Each component (e.g., “number of correct predictions” and “total number of predictions”) is distributive, and the final metric is obtained by dividing or otherwise combining those components.  
- Example: **precision** (correct ÷ total) or **mean rouge‑1** (average of per‑example rouge‑1 scores).  

When you define a metric with `evals.compute_metrics_fn()` / `evals.accumulate_metrics_fn()`, you must mark it as `is_distributive=True` or `is_algebraic=True`. Metrics without a declared type are shown “as is” and do **not** get projected confidence‑interval estimates during online aggregation.

**Traditional sequential execution**

* Runs each configuration **one‑after‑another**.  
* A config must process the **entire dataset for every epoch** (for SFT/RFT) or compute the full evaluation set before the next config can start.  
* No ability to interrupt, swap, or reuse model weights while a run is in flight.  

**RapidFire AI’s adaptive execution engine**

* **Shards** the training/evaluation data into random “chunks” (shards).  
* Schedules **all configs on one shard at a time**, then cycles through the shards, so many configs are active concurrently even on a single GPU.  
* Uses **interruptible execution** and efficient shared‑memory caching (spilling to disk when needed); swapping adapters or base models incurs < 5 % overhead.  
* Provides **online aggregation** of evaluation metrics, giving real‑time estimates and confidence intervals long before the full dataset is processed.  
* Enables **Interactive Control Operations (IC Ops)** – Stop, Resume, Clone, Modify, Warm‑start – allowing you to prune non‑promising runs and launch new variations without restarting the whole experiment.  

**Result:** Multi‑config experiments finish in roughly the same time as a few sequential runs, delivering earlier insights and far more flexible, concurrent exploration.

**RFGridSearch**  
* **Knob values:** each knob may be a single value **or** a `List()` of values. `Range()` is **not allowed** – using it will raise an error.  
* **Behavior:** builds a full grid of every possible combination of the listed values (i.e., exhaustive enumeration).  

**RFRandomSearch**  
* **Knob values:** each knob may be a single value, a `List()` of values **or** a `Range()`.  
* **Behavior:** for each run it samples a value **independently and uniformly** from each knob’s discrete set (`List`) or continuous interval (`Range`). The sampling is IID, repeated until the requested `num_runs` distinct combinations are obtained.  
* **Defaults/extra args:** `num_runs` (required) controls how many sampled combos to generate; `seed` defaults to 42.  

**Key difference:** RFGridSearch only works with fixed lists and exhaustively enumerates them, while RFRandomSearch also accepts ranges and creates a user‑specified number of random combinations.

**Online aggregation** in RapidFire AI evals adapts the database‑research concept of *online aggregation* to LLM evaluation pipelines.  
Instead of waiting for an entire dataset to finish, RapidFire AI shards the data, runs multiple configs in parallel on one shard at a time, and continuously updates metric estimates **with confidence intervals** as each shard is processed. This lets you stop poor‑performing configs early, clone promising ones on the fly, and reach reliable metric estimates much faster.

**Purpose**  
`accumulate_metrics_fn` is an optional user‑provided callback that runs **once, after all batches have been processed**, to combine the per‑batch metric dictionaries produced by `eval.compute_metrics_fn`. It lets you implement custom dataset‑wide aggregation (e.g., weighted averaging, computing accuracy from “Correct” and “Total”, or any other algebraic combination) and to mark the resulting metrics with flags such as `is_algebraic`, `is_distributive`, and `value_range`.

Signature  

```python
def accumulate_metrics_fn(
    aggregated_metrics: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]
) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]:
    ...
```

* `aggregated_metrics` – a mapping from metric name → list of the per‑batch metric dicts (each containing at least the reserved key `"value"`).  
* Return – a dict mapping metric name → a dict that must contain `"value"` and may also include `"is_algebraic"`, `"is_distributive"`, and `"value_range"`.

**If it is not provided**  
The eval system assumes that **all metrics returned by `eval.compute_metrics_fn` are distributive**, meaning they can simply be summed across batches. No custom aggregation is performed; the framework will aggregate by summing the `"value"` fields of each batch.

**`document_template` in `RFLangChainRagSpec`**  
- The template is applied when the RAG spec serializes retrieved documents via `rag.serialize_documents(...)`.  
- For each document, the template determines how the document’s metadata and its text content are combined into a single string that is then inserted into the prompt.  

**Default behavior**  
- If you do **not** supply a custom `document_template`, RapidFire AI falls back to the built‑in template:  

```
"metadata:\ncontent"
```

- In other words, the serialized string for a document consists of the document’s metadata (as a string) followed by a newline (`\n`) and then the document’s raw content.  

**Custom template**  
- You can override this by providing your own `document_template` in the `RFLangChainRagSpec` (e.g., to include a title field or format metadata differently). The custom template will be used instead of the default when `rag.serialize_documents` is called.

Thus, `run_evals()` provides a concrete result object, whereas `run_fit()` is fire‑and‑forget.

**RFPromptManager** builds a prompt by picking the most relevant few‑shot examples for each incoming query.  
The selection works as follows:

1. **Embedding the text** – The manager uses the **`embedding_cfg`** you provide (e.g., `HuggingFaceEmbeddings` or `OpenAIEmbeddings`) to embed both the query and all candidate examples.  

2. **Choosing a selector** – You specify an **`example_selector_cls`**:
   * `SemanticSimilarityExampleSelector` → picks examples that are *most semantically similar* to the query.  
   * `MaxMarginalRelevanceExampleSelector` → picks examples that are both similar and *diverse* (max‑marginal‑relevance).

3. **Retrieving the top‑k examples** – The manager then asks the selector to return **`k`** examples (default = 3). These are the examples that will be inserted into the prompt via the optional `example_prompt_template`.

In short, RFPromptManager embeds the query and the candidate examples, runs either a semantic‑similarity or a max‑marginal‑relevance selector, and returns the top k (default 3) most relevant (or diverse) examples for each input.

A **leaf config** is a single, concrete sub‑section of an evaluation configuration.  
In RapidFire AI, an eval config can contain multiple leaf configs, each representing an individual evaluation scenario (or “run”).  

* Each leaf config can define its own set of user‑provided functions—such as `preprocess_fn`, `postprocess_fn`, etc.—that are injected into the evaluation pipeline.  
* When you call `run_evals()`, the system iterates over the leaf configs and executes a separate run for each one, using the functions and settings defined in that leaf config.  

Thus, a leaf config is the granular unit of configuration that drives a single evaluation run, and multiple leaf configs allow you to run many variations of an evaluation in one call to `run_evals()`.

RapidFire AI says that plain down‑sampling leaves you with several critical shortcomings that its online‑aggregation + IC‑Ops workflow eliminates:

* **You must pick a sample size in advance** – a non‑trivial decision when your evaluation metrics vary a lot across examples.  
* **Down‑sampled results are just point estimates**; they lack statistically‑sound confidence intervals, so you can be falsely confident about a configuration’s performance.  
* **Manual resampling is cumbersome** – you have to generate, store, and juggle many separate sample files if you want to try different sizes or repeats.  
* **No dynamic, on‑the‑fly experimentation** – down‑sampling gives you a static dataset, so you cannot automatically prune bad configs, clone promising ones, or launch new variants while the eval is running. All of that parallel, adaptive control (the “IC Ops” power) would have to be re‑implemented manually.

RapidFire AI’s online aggregation approach provides real‑time metrics, confidence intervals, and automated parallelization, avoiding these downsides while even being usable together with down‑sampling for further cost‑time savings.

4. **Restart the notebook/IDE kernel** and then start the next experiment.

**Distributive metrics** are *purely additive* over the data points that have been seen.  
- They can be summed directly as more shards are processed.  
- Example: a **count** of correct predictions or the **sum** of output‑token lengths.  

**Algebraic metrics** are *averages or proportions* that are computed from separate additive components.  
- Each component (e.g., “number of correct predictions” and “total number of predictions”) is distributive, and the final metric is obtained by dividing or otherwise combining those components.  
- Example: **precision** (correct ÷ total) or **mean rouge‑1** (average of per‑example rouge‑1 scores).  

When you define a metric with `evals.compute_metrics_fn()` / `evals.accumulate_metrics_fn()`, you must mark it as `is_distributive=True` or `is_algebraic=True`. Metrics without a declared type are shown “as is” and do **not** get projected confidence‑interval estimates during online aggregation.
